notes:
Task and constraints: Enumerate all paths from source 0 to target n-1 in a directed acyclic graph.
Idea: Use DFS backtracking, appending each outgoing neighbor to the current path.
Technique and why it applies: Reaching the target copies the path to the results. Otherwise, each neighbor is explored and popped after recursion so sibling paths share no mutations.
Invariant: step is the current path from source to the active node.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty DAG. Multiple paths are preserved as separate result lists.
Complexity: The number of paths can be exponential; work is proportional to traversal plus output size, and recursion depth is O(V).

Task and constraints: Return every path from node 0 to the final node in a DAG.
Idea: Recursively traverse outgoing edges while maintaining a path list.
Technique and why it applies: At the target, path is copied into result. Each other node extends the path through each neighbor, then backtracks by popping that neighbor.
Invariant: path represents the source-to-current-node route; result contains completed routes.
Edge cases: Acyclicity prevents infinite recursion. Copying path protects stored results from later mutations.
Complexity: Path enumeration may be exponential in graph size; auxiliary path and recursion storage is O(V), excluding output.

Task and constraints: Find the rotation with the highest score, where a value scores if it is no greater than its rotated index.
Idea: Maintain qualifying difference thresholds in a heap and update them as rotation increases.
Technique and why it applies: diff[i]=i-nums[i] describes when a value qualifies. Thresholds below the current target are removed; the element shifted from the front is reinserted with its index increased by n.
Invariant: qualified stores the threshold values counted for the current rotation, and its length is the score.
Edge cases: heappush and heappop are used without imports, so the snippet needs those names externally. Ties retain the earliest rotation because the best index changes only on a strictly larger score.
Complexity: Heap updates give O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Return the smallest rotation index with maximum score.
Idea: Use a difference array to record score changes, then prefix-sum it.
Technique and why it applies: For each value, (i-A[i]+1)%N identifies a rotation where its contribution changes. Prefix accumulation gives scores, and index(max) chooses the earliest maximum.
Invariant: change[i] is the score delta at rotation i before the prefix scan.
Edge cases: N must be positive because the code uses modulo N. list.index returns the first occurrence of the maximum.
Complexity: The two passes take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Calculate the champagne amount in glass (r,c) after pouring into the top glass.
Idea: Simulate overflow row by row, cap full glasses at one, and distribute excess equally to the two glasses below.
Technique and why it applies: When quantity exceeds one, prev_flow is split in half between child glasses. A row without overflow ends the simulation early.
Invariant: quantity[(i,j)] stores the amount reaching each glass before its excess is distributed.
Edge cases: The queried row is processed and glasses with overflow are capped at one. defaultdict is used without an import in this snippet, so it must be supplied externally.
Complexity: Processing through row r takes O(r²) time and O(r²) map space.

Task and constraints: Minimize swaps to make both sequences strictly increasing.
Idea: Memoize a recursion by position and whether the previous pair was swapped.
Technique and why it applies: At each index, the code tries keeping the current pair when both values exceed their predecessors, or swapping them when cross-comparisons preserve order. The swap branch adds one.
Invariant: solve returns the minimum future swaps from index i under the effective previous values and swap state.
Edge cases: Initial previous values are -1, relying on positive inputs. The cache key omits previous values, but those are determined by index and the preceding swap decision.
Complexity: O(n) index/state combinations with constant transitions give O(n) time and O(n) memo/stack space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum swaps that make arrays A and B both strictly increasing.
Idea: Use rolling DP states for keeping or swapping the current pair.
Technique and why it applies: Ordinary comparisons allow matching prior states without a swap; cross-comparisons allow a swap transition. Swapped states add one to the number of operations.
Invariant: dp_no_swap and dp_swap store the best costs for the last processed index under each state.
Edge cases: The code initializes the first position to zero swaps or one swap and assumes nonempty arrays.
Complexity: One pass performs constant work per index, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find nodes from which every possible path eventually reaches a terminal node.
Idea: DFS each node and reject a traversal if it revisits a node on its active path.
Technique and why it applies: Encountering a node already in loops proves a cycle. A node is added to ans only after every successor is known safe or successfully traversed.
Invariant: loops is the current recursion path, and ans stores nodes proven safe.
Edge cases: Intermediate results are not memoized, so shared subgraphs may be explored repeatedly. Terminal nodes are added before DFS.
Complexity: Worst-case repeated DFS can be exponential on heavily shared graphs; active-path space is O(V).

Task and constraints: Count bricks that fall after each hit, where stable bricks must connect to the top row.
Idea: Remove hit bricks first, build DSU components, then restore hits backward and measure the roof component's growth.
Technique and why it applies: A virtual roof node represents stability. When a brick is restored, it is unioned with adjacent bricks and the roof if it lies in row zero; newly connected bricks minus the restored one are counted.
Invariant: DSU tracks connected components of present bricks, and sz stores their sizes.
Edge cases: Coordinates that were empty are skipped. Duplicate hits can be mishandled because a later hit on an already removed brick marks that coordinate empty, which may cause the earlier effective hit to be skipped too.
Complexity: Near O((RC+H)α(RC)) time and O(RC) DSU space.

Task and constraints: Count distinct Morse-code representations of words.
Idea: Translate every letter through a fixed Morse dictionary and store each complete encoding as a key.
Technique and why it applies: Concatenating letter codes produces the encoding for a word; the number of distinct keys is the answer.
Invariant: cnt contains one key for each distinct encoded word encountered.
Edge cases: Repeated words or different words with identical encodings do not increase the number of keys. Input words are lowercase.
Complexity: O(total characters) time and O(U) space for U distinct encodings.

Task and constraints: Count unique Morse transformations in a list of words.
Idea: Encode each word by concatenating Morse strings and put the results into a set.
Technique and why it applies: Set membership automatically removes duplicate encodings, regardless of whether the original words are identical.
Invariant: lookup is the set of distinct encodings seen so far.
Edge cases: The list maps lowercase letters by offset from a; characters outside the lowercase alphabet are not supported.
Complexity: Each character is processed once, so time is O(total characters) and storage is O(U) for unique encodings.

Task and constraints: Decide whether an array can be split into two nonempty subsets with equal average.
Idea: Build subset-sum sets indexed by subset size and test whether a subset sum equals the overall average times its size.
Technique and why it applies: Values are processed in reverse subset-size order so each input number is used once. DP[count] stores sums achievable with exactly count elements.
Invariant: DP[count] contains sums for count-element subsets of the processed prefix.
Edge cases: The target uses floating-point division; nonintegral averages cannot match integer sums, while exact integer averages can. Sorting mutates A.
Complexity: The number of reachable subset sums can grow exponentially, so worst-case time and space are exponential in n.

Task and constraints: Check whether a list can be split into subsets with the same average.
Idea: Test possible subset sizes for integer-average feasibility, then construct reachable sums by subset size.
Technique and why it applies: A subset of size i must sum to total*i/n. The DP sets collect sums for each size and the final scan tests the exact target.
Invariant: sums[i] stores sums achievable by i-element subsets of the processed numbers.
Edge cases: The early feasibility call is reversed: possible(n,s) checks n*i divisible by s instead of s*i divisible by n. This can reject valid cases.
Complexity: Subset-sum sets can be exponential in size, so time and space are exponential in n.

Task and constraints: Find the number of lines and the width of the last line when writing a string with given character widths and a 100-unit limit.
Idea: Accumulate character widths and start a new line when the current total exceeds 100.
Technique and why it applies: px tracks the current line width. When adding a character overflows the line, l increases and px resets to that character's width.
Invariant: l counts lines used and px is the current line width.
Edge cases: The code prints each character's ASCII code as a debug side effect. It assumes each character's width is at most 100.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the number of lines needed to write S and the width of the final line.
Idea: Add each character width to the current line, starting a new line if the total would exceed 100.
Technique and why it applies: On overflow, the current character begins the next line, so the line count increments and the width resets to that character's width.
Invariant: result[0] is the number of lines and result[1] is the current line width.
Edge cases: The initialized line count is one, as expected for nonempty S. Character widths are assumed no greater than 100.
Complexity: A single scan takes O(n) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Maximize building heights without changing the city's row and column skylines.
Idea: Compute each row and column maximum, then sum the increase each cell can take.
Technique and why it applies: A cell can rise only to min(row_max,column_max), preserving both skyline views. The difference from its original height is added to ans.
Invariant: mxr[i] and mxc[j] are the original row and column maxima.
Edge cases: The code loops columns using len(grid), assuming a square grid as guaranteed by the task. The comment indentation does not affect the logic.
Complexity: Maxima computation and the sum are O(n²) time with O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Compute the probability soup A empties before soup B, with half credit if both empty together.
Idea: Scale volumes into 25-unit portions and memoize the probability for each remaining pair.
Technique and why it applies: Four equally likely serving operations reduce the two amounts. Base cases return 0.5 when both empty together, 1 when A empties first, and 0 when B empties first.
Invariant: dp(i,j) is the probability that A empties first from remaining scaled amounts i and j.
Edge cases: For n>4451, the method returns 1.0 as an approximation. Otherwise n is rounded up to a 25-unit scale.
Complexity: O(n²) scaled memo states and four transitions per state yield O(n²) time and space.

Task and constraints: Return the soup-serving probability with an approximation for sufficiently large N.
Idea: Use memoized recursion on soup quantities rounded up to units of 25.
Technique and why it applies: Each of four equiprobable operations reduces A and B by different amounts; the recursive result is their average. Base cases handle either or both soups empty.
Invariant: lookup[(a,b)] stores the probability of A emptying first from that state.
Edge cases: N>=4800 returns 1.0 directly. Simultaneous emptying returns 0.5.
Complexity: The memoized state space is O(n²) in scaled units, so time and space are O(n²).

Task and constraints: Count words that can be stretched to match s by expanding repeated-character groups.
Idea: Compress s and each word into character runs and their lengths, then compare corresponding groups.
Technique and why it applies: Character-run sequences must match. A word run cannot exceed the corresponding s run, and unequal run lengths are allowed only when the s run has length at least three.
Invariant: compressor returns the sequence of run characters and their lengths.
Edge cases: The condition's precedence implements (unequal and s-run<3) or word-run>s-run. Empty-case branches return booleans rather than a count, but normal constraints use nonempty strings.
Complexity: Compression and comparisons take O(total characters) time and O(n) temporary space.

Task and constraints: Count the number of strings that can be stretched into s by expanding runs of repeated letters.
Idea: Compare compressed run-character sequences and their run lengths for each candidate word.
Technique and why it applies: A candidate is valid when its run pattern matches s, no run is longer than s's, and any shorter run corresponds to an s run of length at least three.
Invariant: The compressed form preserves each character's identity and the length of its consecutive run.
Edge cases: The implementation's initial empty-input branches return booleans instead of integer counts, though standard constraints are nonempty. The boolean condition relies on Python's and-before-or precedence.
Complexity: Processing each word costs linear time in its length, so total time is O(total characters) and auxiliary space is O(max word length).
